big_idea: People rely on a small set of automatic, evolved mental shortcuts to decide when to comply with a request, and Cialdini's six principles, reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority, and scarcity, explain both why persuasion works and how to recognize and resist manipulation.

tool.label: Reject-Then-Retreat (Door-in-the-Face)
tool.text: Open with a large request you expect to be refused, then follow it with the smaller request you actually wanted. The refusal of the first request triggers a reciprocal sense that the requester has conceded, making the target more likely to accept the second, smaller ask as a fair compromise, and often more likely to agree to related requests later too.
tool.note: Cialdini presents this as an effective persuasion tactic but also explicitly warns readers to watch for it as a manipulation tactic used against them, for example in retail and negotiation settings.

ideas.title: Reciprocity
ideas.text: Giving first, even something small and unsolicited, creates an obligation for the other person to give back.

ideas.title: Commitment and Consistency
ideas.text: After taking a small, especially public or effortful stand, people feel pressure to keep acting consistently with it.

ideas.title: Social Proof
ideas.text: Uncertainty pushes people to copy what others, especially similar others, are doing, powerful, but it can misfire dangerously in emergencies.

ideas.title: Liking
ideas.text: We say yes more readily to people we like, built through similarity, compliments, cooperation, and familiarity.

ideas.title: Authority
ideas.text: Titles, uniforms, and credentials trigger near-automatic deference, sometimes overriding a person's own judgment.

ideas.title: Scarcity
ideas.text: Limited availability or time pressure increases perceived value and urgency to act.

try_it: Before agreeing to a request this week, pause and name which of the six principles, if any, is driving your instinct to say yes.
Practice reciprocity deliberately: do one small, genuine favor for a colleague with no ask attached.
Notice one instance of everyone's doing it marketing this week and evaluate the choice independently of that cue.
Before a negotiation, decide your real target ask in advance so a generous concession from the other side doesn't sway you past it.
best_for: Anyone in sales, marketing, negotiation, or leadership who wants to understand or ethically apply persuasion
People who want to recognize and resist manipulative sales or negotiation tactics
less_useful: Readers looking for cutting-edge research, since the core studies are decades old
Those wanting a step-by-step negotiation playbook rather than a psychology-of-influence explainer

related.why: Cialdini's own follow-up on shaping the moments right before a request
A broader catalog of persuasion laws building on several of these same principles

sources.label: Farnam Street: The Psychology of Persuasion
